doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

chapter: Basie band: origins, sound and style
title: Basie's feeling, Freddie Green and Fiddler Williams
summary: The rhythm section's feel starts with Basie's understated piano; Freddie Green joins in 1937 on Hammond's recommendation, with talk of Fiddler Williams.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Yeah, okay. What was it that made, for you guys, the Basie rhythm section such a, just like the thing to strive for, something about the sound of the band. Was there something specific that those guys were doing?
Well I really can’t say that there was something specific that they were doing differently from anybody else, it’s just the feeling that they got, and I think it started with Basie himself.

His simplistic piano style, and very understated, and a very happy feeling. When he first went to Kansas City and he heard this happy music and he fell in love with it and he wanted to be a part of it, well he, that feeling just osmosed into him and he osmosed it back.
And when they finally added on Freddie Green, Basie was able to give up a lot of stuff with his left hand, and just tinkled, you know and Freddie was going on with the straight 4/4.
1937. I don’t know what month it was, but he joined in 1937. A guy named John Hammond recommended that Basie go down and hear him. Did he go down to some club and hear him?
I’m not sure. I thought he just recommended that he be a part of it. That’s all I know.
And I think at that time, was it Fess Williams that was playing?
Or it wasn’t Eddie Durham, was it?
I don’t think Eddie was playing guitar at that point. If he did it was just occasionally. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Fiddler Williams— And Fiddler Williams is a very brilliant violinist.
Yes he is. He is that.
